content:
Critics of the Quran treat its account of the birth of Jesus (peace be upon him), in Surah Maryam, as a patchwork. The palm tree, they say, comes from a Latin legend, the child who speaks from the cradle from an Arabic infancy gospel, and the title "sister of Aaron" from a confusion of Mary with Miriam, the sister of Moses.[1]

Each piece of the charge can be tested against the texts, and the passage itself can be read as a whole. Read that way, Quran 19:16 to 36 gives the miracle of the birth, and then its meaning, in the words of the child: "I am indeed a servant of Allah" (19:30).[2]

This article aims to provide context to that charge, insha'Allah, in seven details of the passage, set beside the Gospels of Matthew and Luke and the later Christian texts the critics name.

The passage opens: "Relate in the Book (the story of) Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place in the East. She placed a screen (to screen herself) from them; then We sent her our angel, and he appeared before her as a man in all respects" (19:16 to 17).[2]

The Arabic for "our angel" is rūḥanā, "Our Spirit". The verse does not name him, and the classical commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, identify him with Gabriel.[3] Luke 1:26 names Gabriel and sets the scene in Nazareth.[4] The two books agree on the messenger and differ on the setting.

Mary seeks refuge in God, and the messenger answers: "Nay, I am only a messenger from thy Lord, (to announce) to thee the gift of a holy son" (19:18 to 19).[2]

Surah Al ʿImran gives the same annunciation in other words: "O Mary! Allah giveth thee glad tidings of a Word from Him: his name will be Christ Jesus, the son of Mary, held in honour in this world and the Hereafter" (3:45).[2] Luke's angel also names the child Jesus (Luke 1:31). In Luke the child is "the Son of the Most High" (1:32); in the Quran he is a holy son, a sign and a mercy.[4]

"She said: 'How shall I have a son, seeing that no man has touched me, and I am not unchaste?'" The answer: "Thy Lord saith, 'that is easy for Me: and (We wish) to appoint him as a Sign unto men and a Mercy from Us'" (19:20 to 21).[2]

The Quran affirms the virgin conception as plainly as Matthew 1:18 and Luke 1:34 do.[4] The disagreement concerns what the miracle means. The Quran answers in 3:59: "The similitude of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be'. And he was."[2] A birth without a father points to the power of the Creator, as a creation without father or mother did before it.

"And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm-tree: She cried (in her anguish): 'Ah! would that I had died before this! would that I had been a thing forgotten and out of sight!'" A voice answers from beneath her: "Grieve not! for thy Lord hath provided a rivulet beneath thee; and shake towards thyself the trunk of the palm-tree: It will let fall fresh ripe dates upon thee" (19:23 to 25).[2]

The critics' parallel is the Latin Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, where a palm bends to Mary and a spring opens during the flight into Egypt. Its date is disputed: some place it in the early seventh century, others later, and its manuscripts begin in the ninth.[5] A text that may postdate the Quran cannot serve as its source. Suleiman Mourad, comparing the two, argues that the Quranic version need not derive from Pseudo-Matthew and may well be the older telling of a story with roots in earlier, Hellenistic lore.[6] Stephen Shoemaker argues that the Quran's scene reflects a local Palestinian tradition tied to the Kathisma church near Bethlehem, where a rock, a palm and a spring were remembered.[7] Whatever the shared memory, the Quran places the palm at the birth itself, and gives Mary's anguish a voice.

The Arabic does not name the speaker from beneath her. Ibn ʿAbbas took him to be Gabriel; al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada took him to be the child, and al-Tabari preferred their view.[8]

"At length she brought the (babe) to her people, carrying him (in her arms). They said: 'O Mary! truly an amazing thing hast thou brought! O sister of Aaron! Thy father was not a man of evil, nor thy mother a woman unchaste!'" (19:27 to 28).[2]

The objection about Miriam was put to the Prophet's own Companion. Al-Mughira ibn Shuʿba reported that the Christians of Najran asked him how Mary could be called the sister of Aaron when Moses lived long before Jesus. When he asked the Prophet (peace be upon him), the answer was that people used to be named after the prophets and the righteous who had gone before them.[9] Luke 1:5 gives the same kind of naming: Elizabeth, Mary's kinswoman, is "of the daughters of Aaron".[4]

Neither Matthew nor Luke has this scene of return and accusation. Matthew tells the story through Joseph's doubt (Matthew 1:19); Luke through Mary, Elizabeth and the shepherds.[4]

Mary keeps her vow of silence and points to the child. "They said: 'How can we talk to one who is a child in the cradle?' He said: 'I am indeed a servant of Allah: He hath given me revelation and made me a prophet; and He hath made me blessed wheresoever I be, and hath enjoined on me Prayer and Charity as long as I live; (He) hath made me kind to my mother'" (19:29 to 32).[2]

The Arabic Gospel of the Infancy, which survives in Arabic manuscripts of the thirteenth century and later, also has Jesus speak in the cradle. There he tells Mary: "I am Jesus, the Son of God, the Logos."[10] The two speeches share a setting and say opposite things.

Cornelia Horn, studying the passages of Quran 3 and 19 beside the Protoevangelium of James, finds striking parallels and no direct evidence that the Quran used any text of the infancy-gospel genre as a source.[11] The child's words carry the Quran's own verdict.

"Such (was) Jesus the son of Mary: (it is) a statement of truth, about which they (vainly) dispute. It is not befitting to (the majesty of) Allah that He should beget a son. Glory be to Him! when He determines a matter, He only says to it, 'Be', and it is" (19:34 to 35).[2]

The last words return to the child: "Verily Allah is my Lord and your Lord: Him therefore serve ye: this is a Way that is straight" (19:36).[2] The story interprets its own miracle. The birth raises Jesus to honour, and the honour is that of a servant and prophet of the One who said "Be".

The bottom line

The charge of a patchwork does not hold. The Latin palm legend may be later than the Quran; the infancy gospel's speaking child proclaims a theology the Quran's child denies; and the question of "sister of Aaron" was answered in the Prophet's lifetime, with a usage Luke himself shares.

What remains is a narrative with its own shape: withdrawal, annunciation, virgin conception, the palm, the accusation and the child's defence of his mother. Muslims and Christians agree on the virgin birth. The Quran adds the conclusion the passage was told to give, "Such (was) Jesus the son of Mary", a servant of God and His prophet. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The argument is common in missionary and critical writing; for its classic statement see William St Clair Tisdall, The Original Sources of the Qur'an (London: SPCK, 1905), chapter 4.
  2. Quran 19:16 to 36; 3:45; 3:59, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-ʿAzim, on Quran 19:17.
  4. Luke 1:5, 1:26 to 38; Matthew 1:18 to 25 (World English Bible).
  5. Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew 20 to 21. On its date, see the North American Society for the Study of Christian Apocryphal Literature, e-Clavis: Christian Apocrypha, "Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew".
  6. Suleiman A. Mourad, "From Hellenism to Christianity and Islam: The Origin of the Palm Tree Story Concerning Mary and Jesus in the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew and the Qur'ān", Oriens Christianus 86 (2002), 206 to 216.
  7. Stephen J. Shoemaker, "Christmas in the Qur'ān: The Qur'ānic Account of Jesus' Nativity and Palestinian Local Tradition", Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam 28 (2003).
  8. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-ʿAzim, on Quran 19:24, reporting the views and al-Tabari's preference; al-Tabari, Jamiʿ al-bayan ʿan taʾwil ay al-Qurʾan, on the same verse.
  9. Sahih Muslim 2135; Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 3155.
  10. The Arabic Gospel of the Infancy of the Saviour 1, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 8, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson.
  11. Cornelia B. Horn, "Intersections: The Reception History of the Protoevangelium of James in Sources from the Christian East and in the Qur'ān", Apocrypha 17 (2006), 113 to 150.
